sections.title: A palace, a border and a 1,700 km detour
sections.intro_md:
Stand on the lawn of Ujjayanta Palace in Agartala and the Bangladesh border is about 2 km away. Before 1947 it did not exist. A trader could go from Agartala to Calcutta in under 350 km, across the flat rice country of East Bengal. Then Partition drew a frontier around three sides of the old princely state, and the road to Calcutta became a 1,700 km loop north through Assam and the Siliguri neck. For sixty years Tripura was one of India's most cut-off corners, with no railway to its capital until 2008.

That is the paradox at the heart of today. Tripura is tiny, the third-smallest state, yet it carries one of the longest unbroken royal stories in Asia, a Bengali-speaking majority and nineteen indigenous peoples, a goddess temple from 1501 and a forest of rock-cut gods older than that. It is also a place where a border shapes almost everything: who lives here, what they eat, how they vote and which way the trucks go.

spotlights.name: Agartala
spotlights.spot_it: A low, green capital on the Haora river, 2 km from Bangladesh, with a railway station built to look like a palace.
spotlights.story_md: The name joins agar, the fragrant agarwood tree, with tala, meaning underneath: the town under the agar trees. The kings moved their court here from Udaipur in stages; the modern city was laid out from 1849, and Bir Chandra Manikya created its municipality in 1871, when it had 875 residents in 8 square km. Today Greater Agartala has over half a million people and is the second-largest city in the North East after Guwahati. Because Bangladesh is so close, Agartala became India's third international internet gateway, with bandwidth brought in across the border from Bangladesh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The capital sits so close to the border that the border is part of daily life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under the agar trees, two kilometres from another country.

sections.title: Tripura in eight numbers
sections.intro_md:
Tripura covers 10,492 square km, smaller than Kerala's Idukki and Ernakulam districts put together, and only Goa and Sikkim are smaller among the states. It is about 178 km from north to south and 131 km across. Bangladesh wraps it on the north, west and south along an 856 km border; Assam and Mizoram touch only its eastern edge.

The 2011 census counted 3.67 million people, second in the North East after Assam, packed at 350 per square km. Roughly two-thirds are Bengali-speaking, most of them descended from refugees who came after 1947 and 1971. Nearly a third, 31.8 percent, belong to 19 Scheduled Tribes. Hindus are 83 percent, Muslims about 9, Christians 4 and Buddhists 3.

One more number matters. About 68 percent of the land lies inside the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council, a self-governing tribal zone under the Sixth Schedule, while most people live in the smaller, flatter west.

spotlights.name: The border haats
spotlights.spot_it: Open sheds right on the zero line, with Indian sellers on one side, Bangladeshi sellers on the other and a Kali temple on the hill above.
spotlights.story_md: A border haat is a weekly market built on the international line, where people living within a few kilometres on either side can buy and sell local goods without a passport. At Kamalasagar, about 27 km from Agartala, the market sits under a hill crowned by a Kali temple that looks straight across the fence into Bangladesh, toward Kasba railway station. Tripura has several such haats. They are a small, practical admission that the border cut through one market region: the same vegetables, fish, saris and plastic buckets used to move freely along these roads.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how the 1947 line cut through a single economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: A market where the border runs down the middle aisle.

sections.title: Five ridges, wet valleys and drowned forests
sections.intro_md:
Tripura looks like a rumpled bedsheet. Five long hill ranges run north to south: Baramura (Hathai Kotor) in the west, then Atharamura, Longtharai, Shakhan and, on the Mizoram border, Jampui. Between them lie narrow valleys, and in the west the land flattens into the plain around Agartala. Small isolated hillocks are called tillas; the narrow wet valley floors are lungas. Rice grows in the lungas, rubber and pineapple on the tillas.

Almost every river starts in these hills and flows out into Bangladesh: the Khowai, Dhalai and Manu north to the Barak and Meghna system, the Gumti and Haora west, the Feni south-west. Rain is heavy, about 2,000 to 2,700 mm a year, and floods are common. Rudrasagar Lake near Melaghar, home of the water palace, is a Ramsar wetland of international importance.

The state lies in seismic zone V, the highest risk category. An earthquake in 1897 destroyed the old royal palace, which is why the present one stands where it does.

spotlights.name: Jampui Hills
spotlights.when: Settled by Mizo people from the 16th century
spotlights.spot_it: A long ridge at about 1,000 m on the Mizoram border, lined with Mizo villages, churches and orange groves.
spotlights.story_md: The eastern ridge is Tripura's high country. It averages about 1,000 m, and its southern summit, Betling Shib, also called Thaidawr Tlang, is the state's highest point at roughly 930 to 939 m. Ten villages run along the crest, mostly Mizo and Christian, with Vanghmun as the block headquarters. Families grow oranges, betel nut, ginger and coffee; the Jampui orange festival each November is the hills' big event. On a clear morning you can see across into Mizoram, and the dawn view over a sea of valley mist is the reason most visitors make the long drive up from Kanchanpur.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The highest and coolest corner of a hot, low state, and a Mizo enclave inside Tripura.
spotlights.memory_hook: Oranges, churches and Tripura's rooftop at about 930 m.

compare.difference: Jampui's Mizo villages keep the bamboo-pole Cheraw dance of Mizoram alive inside Tripura.

spotlights.name: The Gumti (Gomati) River
spotlights.when: Sacred river; dammed at Dumboor in the 1970s
spotlights.spot_it: A slow brown river winding through Udaipur, the old royal capital, toward Comilla in Bangladesh.
spotlights.story_md: The Gumti is Tripura's biggest river and the spine of its history. It rises in the eastern hills at Dumboor, where a pilgrimage called the Pous Sankranti mela gathers at Tirthamukh every 14 January. It then cuts west through the Atharamura range, past the cliff carvings of Chabimura, through Udaipur, which was the Manikya capital for centuries, and on into Bangladesh, where Comilla city sits on its banks. Its name, Gomati, is shared with a sacred river of North India. Floods on the Gumti hit both countries, which makes the river a recurring diplomatic subject.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The river joins the old capital, the hill shrines and the Bangladesh plain.
spotlights.memory_hook: From the drowned forest to Comilla: one river, two countries.

spotlights.name: Dumboor Lake
spotlights.when: Reservoir behind the Gumti hydel dam
spotlights.spot_it: A wide reservoir dotted with 48 wooded islets, shaped by legend like the damru drum of Shiva.
spotlights.story_md: Dumboor is a reservoir of about 41 square km behind the Gumti hydroelectric dam, with 48 islets inside it. Its name comes from the damru, the small hourglass drum carried by Shiva, which the lake's outline is said to resemble. It lies inside the Gumti Wildlife Sanctuary, a forest of 390 square km, and winter brings migratory ducks. The dam has never been popular. Flooding the valley in the 1970s displaced thousands of tribal families. In August 2024, when floods swamped eastern Bangladesh, rumours there blamed water released from Dumboor; India's foreign ministry replied that the dam lay more than 120 km upstream and that rain in the catchment below it caused the flooding.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A beauty spot that is also a symbol of displacement and cross-border suspicion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shiva's drum, 48 islands and a lot of blame.

sections.title: Spectacled monkeys and a cloud-spotted cat
sections.intro_md:
More than half of Tripura is forest. The 2011 figure was about 58 percent; later satellite surveys, counting plantations and tree cover more broadly, put it higher. Bamboo and cane run through almost every forest type, which is unusual even for the North East.

The state is a primate stronghold. A survey cited by the state counted seven of India's free-ranging primate species here, including the hoolock gibbon, the capped langur, the slow loris and the spectacled Phayre's leaf monkey, which is now the state animal. Elephants, gaur, clouded leopards, binturongs and around 300 bird species share the forest. The wild buffalo is already gone. The state bird, the green imperial pigeon, is a big fruit-eater of the canopy, and the state tree is the agar.

The protected network is small, about 567 square km in all: Sepahijala, Gumti, Rowa and Trishna sanctuaries, and two national parks, Clouded Leopard and Rajbari.

spotlights.name: Phayre's leaf monkey
spotlights.spot_it: A slim grey langur with bright white rings around its eyes, as if wearing spectacles.
spotlights.story_md: Bengali speakers call it chasma bandor, the spectacled monkey, for the broad white rings around its eyes and its pale mouth. It lives high in the canopy and eats mostly leaves; in Tripura its menu includes leaves of siris trees, bamboo, ficus and jackfruit relatives. The species is classed as Endangered, hit by hunting and by forest loss. Tripura made it the state animal, and Sepahijala is the easiest place to see one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state chose an endangered leaf-eater as its emblem.
spotlights.memory_hook: The monkey that wears its glasses on its fur.

spotlights.name: Clouded Leopard National Park
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny forest park 28 km from Agartala named after a cat with cloud-shaped blotches.
spotlights.story_md: The national park covers only about 5 square km inside the 18.5 square km Sepahijala Wildlife Sanctuary, which was declared in 1987. It is named after the clouded leopard, a secretive tree-climbing cat with the longest canine teeth for its size of any living cat and a coat of large dark blotches edged like clouds. You are unlikely to see one in the wild here. You will see the four primate species the park is known for, including Phayre's langur, and the sanctuary's lakes, zoo and research centre.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A pocket of forest close to the capital where people meet Tripura's wildlife.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five square kilometres named for a cat almost nobody sees.

sections.title: Nineteen peoples and a Bengali majority
sections.intro_md:
For most of its history Tripura was a Tripuri kingdom whose people spoke Kokborok, a Tibeto-Burman language related to Bodo and Garo. In 1941 the princely state had about 513,000 people, mostly tribal. Partition changed that in two waves. Between 1947 and 1951 roughly 610,000 Hindu Bengalis fled East Pakistan into Tripura, almost as many as already lived there. In 1971 a second, larger wave arrived. Most stayed. Tribal communities, once the majority, became a third of the population, and that shift drives Tripura's politics to this day.

The 19 Scheduled Tribes are not one group. The largest is the Tripuri (Debbarma and related clans), over half the tribal population, followed by the Reang or Bru, the Jamatia, the Chakma, the Halam, the Mog (Marma), and smaller groups such as the Noatia, Garo, Kuki, Lushai, Darlong, Munda and Santal, the last two brought as tea labour. Bengali is the main language; Kokborok has been an official language since 1979.

spotlights.name: Kokborok

where.label: Spoken across Tripura and the Chittagong Hill Tracts

spotlights.spot_it: A tonal Tibeto-Burman language; 'kok' means speech and 'borok' means people.
spotlights.story_md: Kokborok belongs to the Bodo-Garo branch, cousin to Bodo and Dimasa in Assam and Garo in Meghalaya. Tradition says the royal chronicle was first written in a Kokborok script called Koloma, now lost; under the kings Bengali became the court language and Kokborok was pushed to the villages. The state made it official in 1979, and it is now taught from primary school to an MA at Tripura University (since 2015). The script is the fight. The Left Front backed Bengali letters; tribal parties and student groups want the Roman alphabet, which the tribal council adopted for its schools in 1992 and 2000. Both are in use, and new scripts keep being proposed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Whether you write it in Bengali or Roman letters is a political statement.
spotlights.memory_hook: One language, two alphabets, one old argument.

spotlights.name: The Bru who came back
spotlights.spot_it: The Reang, who call themselves Bru, are Tripura's second-largest tribe, and some lived 23 years in relief camps.
spotlights.story_md: In October 1997 ethnic violence in western Mizoram drove more than 30,000 Bru across the border into North Tripura. They lived for over two decades in crowded relief camps around Kanchanpur on government rations. Repeated attempts to send them back failed; the camps recorded more deaths than births in some years. On 16 January 2020 the Centre, Tripura, Mizoram and Bru leaders signed a four-way agreement to settle about 34,000 people permanently in Tripura instead. The Bru are also the community behind Hojagiri, the pitcher-balancing dance, so the camps held one of the region's best-known art forms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The longest internal displacement in the North East ended with resettlement, not return.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-three years in a camp, then a new address.

spotlights.name: Bizu, the Chakma new year

where.label: Chakma villages of North and Dhalai districts

spotlights.spot_it: Flowers floated on the river at dawn, then three days of visiting, cooking and a dance with sudden pauses.
spotlights.story_md: The Chakma, Buddhist and spread across Tripura, Mizoram and Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts, mark the end of the Bengali year with Bizu. Day one, Phool Bizu, is for cleaning houses, decking them with flowers and floating blossoms on the water. Day two, Mul Bizu, is for visiting every house in the village and eating a special mixed vegetable curry, pajon, with as many ingredients as possible. Day three, Gojjepojje, is for religious and social duties. The Bizu dance is done in a square or circle and is known for its abrupt stops. Chakma belief says a person who dies on Mul Bizu goes to heaven.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of several April new years that link Tripura to Southeast Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: Flowers on the river, a hundred vegetables in the pot.

spotlights.name: Sangrai of the Mog
spotlights.spot_it: Young people splashing each other with water from bowls and buckets, in the style of Thai Songkran.
spotlights.story_md: The Mog, also called Marma, are Buddhists of Arakanese origin living mostly in the far south around Sabroom. Their new year, Sangrai, falls in mid-April and shares its water-throwing with Songkran in Thailand and Thingyan in Myanmar: splashing washes away the old year. They also hold Owa, the end of the Buddhist rains retreat, on the full moon of Ashwin, floating small paper or toy boats on the river.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Tripura's cultural line runs east into Myanmar and Thailand, not only west to Bengal.
spotlights.memory_hook: A water fight that carries the new year across four countries.

sections.title: One dynasty, five centuries
sections.intro_md:
The Manikya kings ruled from about 1400 until 1949, one of the longest-running royal houses in South Asia. Their own chronicle, the Rajmala, stretches the line back to the Moon and lists 179 kings; historians accept only the later part. Coins suggest the first real Manikya was Maha Manikya in the early 1400s, a Tripuri chief who united neighbouring clans and took the title after a victory over Bengal.

At its peak in the 16th century, under Dhanya Manikya and Vijaya Manikya II, the kingdom ran from the Garo Hills to the Bay of Bengal and fought the Sultans of Bengal and the kings of Arakan. The Mughals took the plains in the 17th and 18th centuries but never held the hills. In 1809 Tripura became a British protectorate. The kings kept their hill state, called Hill Tippera, plus a rich estate on the plains, Chakla Roshnabad, around today's Comilla in Bangladesh, and they became great patrons of Bengali culture.

data.name: Vijaya Manikya II
data.note: Height of power, coins in his name

spotlights.name: The Rajmala
spotlights.when: Begun in the 15th century, compiled to the 19th
spotlights.spot_it: A royal chronicle in Bengali verse, written and rewritten over four centuries.
spotlights.story_md: The Rajmala, the garland of kings, was commissioned by Dharma Manikya I in the 15th century from the royal priest Durlabhendra and two Brahmin scholars, Sukheshwar and Baneshwar. Later parts were added under Amar Manikya, Govinda Manikya, Krishna Manikya and Kashi Chandra Manikya, and the whole was compiled in the mid-19th century. It traces the kings from Chandra, the Moon, through Druhyu, son of the epic king Yayati, and a mythical tyrant named Tripur. Historians use it carefully: its early genealogy is legendary, and some reigns are confused or duplicated. Still, it is the main written source for the kingdom's history, and it is also a monument of early Bengali literature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dynasty wrote its own history, and historians still argue about which parts to believe.
spotlights.memory_hook: A garland of 179 kings, some of them real.

spotlights.name: Vijaya Manikya II
spotlights.spot_it: Known today mostly through his silver coins: a lion on one face, Bengali script naming the king on the other.
spotlights.story_md: Vijaya came to the throne as a boy, a puppet of his army commander, and then, according to the chronicle, had the commander killed and took power himself. He reorganised the army with archers, elephants, artillery, a river navy and Afghan cavalry; the chronicle's figure of 200,000 infantry, 1,000 elephants and 5,000 boats is surely inflated. He raided deep into the Bengal Sultanate and under him Tripura reached its widest extent. The kings struck coins in silver and gold with a lion, the royal emblem, and dates in the Saka era. A coin dated 1560 is shown here.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Coins are the hard evidence for a kingdom whose chronicle mixes myth and fact.
spotlights.memory_hook: A boy king, a murdered general and a lion on every coin.

spotlights.name: Govinda Manikya and the end of sacrifice
spotlights.spot_it: A small Bengal-style temple on the Gumti bank, next to the ruins of his palace, made famous by Tagore.
spotlights.story_md: Govinda was overthrown within a year by his brother, who had Mughal backing, and fled to the Chittagong hills and then to Arakan, whose king helped him back to the throne in 1667. To keep peace with the Mughals he sent five elephants a year as tribute. He is remembered as a patron of learning: the third part of the Rajmala was finished in his reign. Two centuries later Tagore turned him into a moral hero. In the novel Rajarshi and the play Bisarjan, Govinda bans animal sacrifice at the temple and defies his priest. The Bhubaneswari temple at Udaipur, built around his time, is the setting.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A real king became the voice of Tagore's argument against blood sacrifice.
spotlights.memory_hook: The king who, in Tagore's version, said no more blood.

spotlights.name: Bir Chandra Manikya, the photographer king
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian-era king who took his own photographs, including portraits of his queen.
spotlights.story_md: Bir Chandra rebuilt his state on the British model and founded the Agartala municipality in 1871. He was also one of India's earliest serious photographers. He held an annual photographic exhibition at his palace, the first such royal show in India, and was a member of the Royal Photographic Society from 1896. More than a century after his death, his fully equipped studio, his 'photo karkhana', was found inside the palace. After his queen died in 1881, he read the young Rabindranath Tagore's poem Bhagna Hriday, found his own grief in it and sent his secretary to Calcutta to congratulate the poet, then about 20, and offer him a printing press. It began a friendship between the two families.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made Agartala modern and made the first royal bet on Tagore.
spotlights.memory_hook: A king behind the camera, a poet in his post.

spotlights.name: Radha Kishore Manikya
spotlights.spot_it: The king beside Tagore in a 1900 photograph, builder of the white palace in Agartala.
spotlights.story_md: Radha Kishore took over just after the 1897 earthquake had wrecked the old palace and he still spent 10 lakh rupees, a huge sum, building Ujjayanta in the centre of Agartala. He separated the police from revenue collection, gave Visva-Bharati a yearly grant and funded schools and colleges, including Victoria College in Comilla and a wing of R. G. Kar Medical College in Calcutta. The story most often told about him: when the scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose needed money for his research, the king, short of cash, pledged his daughter-in-law's jewellery to fund him anonymously.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small hill kingdom quietly paid for Bengal's science and art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Jewels pawned for a scientist, a palace built after an earthquake.

spotlights.name: Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya
spotlights.spot_it: The last ruling king: built the airport in 1942, the water palace and the land reserve that became the tribal council area.
spotlights.story_md: Bir Bikram is called the architect of modern Tripura. He was the first Tripura king to travel to Europe and America, in 1931 and 1939. In 1942 he built an airfield at Singerbhil outside Agartala; within a year the RAF was using it to supply the Chindit raids behind Japanese lines in Burma, and American transport squadrons followed. Today it is Maharaja Bir Bikram Airport, the second busiest in the North East. He also reserved land for the indigenous Tiprasa, the root of today's tribal council area, founded the college that bears his name, and built Neermahal. He died on 17 May 1947, three months before independence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His decisions still shape Tripura's map, airport and politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: A runway for the Burma war that became Tripura's front door.

spotlights.name: Kanchan Prabha Devi and the merger
spotlights.spot_it: The queen mother who signed away a kingdom on behalf of her 15-year-old son.
spotlights.story_md: When Bir Bikram died in May 1947, his heir Kirit Bikram Kishore was 13. A Council of Regency led by his widow, Kanchan Prabha Devi, a princess of Panna in central India, ran the state through Partition, communal violence on the borders and a feared push from East Pakistan. Tripura acceded to India on 13 August 1947. On 9 September 1949 she signed the merger agreement, and on 15 October 1949 Tripura became a Part C state governed from Delhi. Kirit Bikram, the last king, later sat three times in the Lok Sabha. The family's head today is his son Pradyot, a politician.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A regent's signature ended five centuries of Manikya rule.
spotlights.memory_hook: One signature, five hundred years.

sections.title: Tagore, two palaces and a prince who wrote film songs
sections.intro_md:
The Manikyas were Tripuri kings, but from the 19th century their court spoke, wrote and dreamed in Bengali. That made Agartala a small outpost of the Bengal Renaissance, and the link ran through one family in particular: the Tagores of Jorasanko.

Rabindranath Tagore visited Tripura seven times between about 1900 and 1926. Three of his works, the novel Rajarshi and the plays Bisarjan and Mukut, draw on Tripura's royal history. The kings, from Bir Chandra to Bir Bikram, paid a yearly grant to his university at Santiniketan, and Tripura's money helped bring Manipuri dance into its curriculum.

The same court produced the palaces that now define the state's image, and, through a younger branch of the royal family, one of the great composers of Hindi cinema.

rows.Ujjayanta Palace: Centre of Agartala, between two lakes

rows.Neermahal: Hindu and Mughal mix, minarets and kiosks

spotlights.name: Rabindranath Tagore in Tripura
spotlights.spot_it: The bearded poet in a long robe, here in 1926, the year he last stayed in Agartala at Pushpabanta Palace.
spotlights.story_md: Tagore's tie to Tripura began with a fan letter from a king: Bir Chandra Manikya's congratulations on Bhagna Hriday in the early 1880s. He first visited in 1900, during Radha Kishore's reign, and came back in 1919 for a celebration of his Nobel Prize. His seventh and last visit was in February 1926, when he stayed at Pushpabanta Palace and wrote poems and songs. He wrote at least five songs in Tripura. The court gave him plots too: Rajarshi and Bisarjan retell the story of Govinda Manikya. In May 1941 King Bir Bikram held a celebration for his 80th birthday and gave him the title Bharat Bhaskar, months before the poet died.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The friendship turned a hill court into a patron of Bengal's greatest writer.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven visits, five songs, one royal fan club.

spotlights.name: Ujjayanta Palace
spotlights.spot_it: A long white two-storey palace with three domes, the tallest 26 m, behind formal gardens and two lakes.
spotlights.story_md: After the 1897 earthquake ruined the old palace outside town, Radha Kishore Manikya built this one in the centre of Agartala for 10 lakh rupees. It was designed by Sir Alexander Martin of the Calcutta firm Martin and Burn, in Indo-Saracenic style with Mughal, Roman and British touches, and its name, meaning the one who has conquered, is said to have been given by Tagore. It was the royal home until 1949. The state bought it in 1972 to 1973 and used it as the Legislative Assembly until 2011. Since 2013 it has been the Tripura State Museum, with 22 galleries, sculptures from Pilak and Unakoti, royal coins and the arts of the whole North East.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A royal palace that became a parliament and then a museum.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built after an earthquake, named by a poet, ruled from until 2011.

spotlights.name: Neermahal, the water palace
spotlights.spot_it: A long red and white palace with domed kiosks and minarets that seems to float in the middle of a lake.
spotlights.story_md: Bir Bikram Kishore Manikya commissioned Martin and Burn to build a summer palace in Rudrasagar Lake, about 53 km from Agartala, and worked on the design himself. Sources put the start around 1921 and completion in the early 1930s, with work said to have taken about nine years. It has 24 rooms. The western half, the Andar Mahal, was for the royal family; the eastern half held an open-air stage for drama and dance. The king reached it by hand-rowed boat from Rajghat. It is the largest water palace in India and the only one in the east. Each August a three-day Neermahal Water Festival brings boat races and swimming contests to the lake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Tripura's most photographed building and a sign of royal ambition in the last decades of rule.
spotlights.memory_hook: Row out to dinner, watch a play, row home.

spotlights.name: S. D. Burman, the prince of film music
spotlights.spot_it: A thin, high, folk-inflected voice; listen for 'Wahan Kaun Hai Tera' from Guide (1965), sung by the composer himself.
spotlights.story_md: Sachin Dev Burman was born on 1 October 1906 in the Tripura royal family's palace at Comilla, son of Prince Nabadwipchandra and grandson of Maharaja Ishan Chandra Manikya; his mother was a Manipuri princess. He studied in Comilla and Calcutta, trained in classical music, and grew up absorbing the boatmen's and folk songs of East Bengal. Accounts say he broke with the royal family, partly over his marriage to his student Meera Das Gupta. He went on to compose for more than 100 Bengali and Hindi films, from Pyaasa to Guide and Aradhana. His son, R. D. Burman, became an even bigger name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hindi film music's most distinctive folk sound came out of the Tripura court.
spotlights.memory_hook: A prince who swapped a throne for a harmonium.

sections.title: Gods in stone: temples, cliffs and a mountain of faces
sections.intro_md:
Tripura's oldest art is carved into its hills. At Unakoti in the north, rock faces were cut into gods and goddesses between the 7th and 9th centuries. At Pilak in the south, Buddhist and Hindu images lie side by side in terracotta and sandstone. At Chabimura, a goddess 6 m tall stares down at the Gumti from a vertical cliff. Together they show that this corner of India sat on a crossroads of Bengal's Pala and Gupta styles, Arakanese Buddhism and local tribal practice.

The state is even named after a goddess. Tripura Sundari's temple at Udaipur, built in 1501, is one of the 51 Shakti Pithas, where the body of the goddess Sati is said to have fallen in pieces. Most Hindus in Tripura are Shakta or Vaishnava Bengalis; the royal family combined Hindu worship with tribal deities, and that blend still shows in festivals like Kharchi Puja.

spotlights.name: Unakoti
spotlights.spot_it: A 9 m high face of Shiva cut into a forest cliff, with a 3 m headdress and goddesses on either side.
spotlights.story_md: Unakoti means one less than a crore. Legend says Shiva stopped here for a night on the way to Kashi with 9,999,999 gods and told them to wake before dawn. Only he woke, so he cursed the rest into stone. A local version credits a sculptor, Kallu, who had to carve a crore images in one night to earn a place on Mount Kailash and fell one short. The real carvings, dated on style to the 7th to 9th centuries, include the central Shiva head, Unakotiswara Kal Bhairava, about 9 m high, huge Ganesha figures and Nandi bulls half-sunk in the ground. It entered UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in 2022.
spotlights.why_it_matters: North East India's largest rock-relief site and a candidate for World Heritage status.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ninety-nine lakh, ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine sleepers.

spotlights.name: Tripura Sundari temple (Matabari)
spotlights.spot_it: A cube-shaped red temple with a three-tiered curved Bengal roof on a small hill shaped like a tortoise's back.
spotlights.story_md: Dhanya Manikya built the shrine in 1501, after the goddess, the legend says, appeared to him in a dream twice. The hill it stands on resembles a tortoise's hump, which makes it a Kurma Pitha, the holiest possible ground for a Shakti temple. Tradition says the toes of Sati's right foot fell here. Inside are two black stone images: Tripura Sundari, about 1.5 m tall, and the small Chhoto Ma, which the kings carried into battle and on hunts. The Diwali fair draws more than 200,000 pilgrims, and the prasad, a milk sweet called Matabari peda, received a GI tag in 2024. On 22 September 2025 the Prime Minister opened a rebuilt complex funded under the PRASHAD scheme.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The temple gives the state its name and is the busiest pilgrimage in the North East after Kamakhya.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess on a tortoise, guarded by turtles.

spotlights.name: The turtles of Kalyan Sagar
spotlights.spot_it: Big dark softshell turtles surfacing at the steps of the temple tank to take food from pilgrims.
spotlights.story_md: Below the temple lies Kalyan Sagar, a tank of about 6.4 acres. It holds black softshell turtles, Nilssonia nigricans, a species once thought extinct in the wild and now known from only a handful of places, almost all of them temple and shrine ponds in Bangladesh and North East India. Because they are sacred, nobody eats them, which is likely the only reason they survive. Conservationists now raise hatchlings from such ponds and release them, a rare case of religion doing a wildlife reserve's job.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Temple ponds are among the last refuges of a critically threatened turtle.
spotlights.memory_hook: Holy water, holy turtles, almost nowhere else.

spotlights.name: Chabimura (Devtamura)
spotlights.spot_it: A towering Durga cut into a sheer river cliff, seen from a boat on the Gumti.
spotlights.story_md: Chabimura, the hill of images, also called Devtamura, is a stretch of near-vertical cliffs on the Gumti near Amarpur, about 82 km from Agartala. Carved into the rock are Shiva, Vishnu, Kartikeya, Ganesha and a Mahishasuramardini Durga about 6 m tall, dated to the 15th and 16th centuries, during Manikya rule. In Kokborok the place is Chakrakma. The panels are reached by boat from Chabimura ghat through jungle-lined water, which is part of the experience. Few visitors make the trip.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the Manikya era continuing a much older habit of carving gods into cliffs.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess you can only meet by boat.

spotlights.name: Pilak
spotlights.spot_it: Low brick stupa mounds and terracotta plaques of Buddhas, gods and animals in paddy country near the Bangladesh border.
spotlights.story_md: Pilak spreads over about 10 square km near Jolaibari, 100 km south of Agartala. Finds since 1927 include brick stupas and a monastery, terracotta plaques and stone images of the Buddha, Avalokiteshvara, Marichi and Hindu deities such as Surya and Narasimha. The style mixes Pala and Gupta Bengal, Arakan and local hands. Pilak belongs to the old Samatata region, the same cultural zone as Mainamati near Comilla in Bangladesh. Some images are still worshipped: an 8th to 9th century Buddhist goddess Marichi stands in a Hindu temple, and an 18-armed Chunda is revered as Raja Rajeshwari.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that Tripura was part of Bengal's Buddhist world a thousand years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Buddhas in a paddy field, goddesses who changed religion.

sections.title: Refugees, a war next door and a case named after Agartala
sections.intro_md:
Partition hit Tripura harder than almost any part of India except Punjab and Bengal themselves. The kings lost their plains estate to East Pakistan. Roads, rivers and markets that had run west to Comilla and Chittagong were cut. And people came. Hindu Bengalis fleeing violence and discrimination in East Pakistan arrived in waves after 1947, 1950 and 1964, and then in a flood in 1971.

During Bangladesh's war of independence Tripura became the rear base of the Mukti Bahini, the liberation army. Training camps, field hospitals and the exiled leadership used Agartala and its border towns. Pakistani artillery shelled border areas. At the peak, the number of refugees in Tripura roughly matched the state's own population of about 1.5 million.

The second wave settled for good. In one generation, the tribal majority of the princely state became a minority, and the anger that followed fuelled an insurgency.

visual.title: Tripura's population, and the refugees it absorbed (thousands)

spotlights.name: The year Tripura doubled

where.label: Border camps around Agartala and Sonamura

spotlights.spot_it: Columns of families with bundles walking in from the west; camps in schools, fields and tea gardens.
spotlights.story_md: From March 1971, when the Pakistani army cracked down in East Pakistan, refugees crossed into Tripura by the hundreds of thousands. Estimates of the peak run from about 1 million to 1.5 million, in a state whose own population was around 1.5 to 1.6 million: for months, almost every second person in Tripura was a refugee. Locals shared food, schools became camps, and the state government ran on emergency funds. Families of Bangladesh's future leaders sheltered here, including that of Tajuddin Ahmad, the wartime prime minister; in 2021 his daughter, by then an MP, came back to Sonamura to say thank you. Most 1971 refugees returned after December, but many earlier migrants stayed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Few places anywhere have absorbed a crowd as big as themselves in a single year.
spotlights.memory_hook: For a few months, every other person was a guest.

spotlights.name: The Agartala Conspiracy Case
spotlights.spot_it: A 1968 treason trial in Pakistan against Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, named after the Indian town where the plot was said to have been hatched.
spotlights.story_md: In 1968 Ayub Khan's government charged Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and 34 others with conspiring with India to break East Pakistan away. The case was named after Agartala because two of the accused had allegedly travelled there to meet Indian officials. It backfired. Mass protests in 1969 forced Pakistan to drop the case, freed Mujib and made him the undisputed leader of East Bengal, two years before independence. For decades it was called a frame-up, but in 2011 one of the accused, Shawkat Ali, told Bangladesh's parliament that the charges had been true.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small Indian town gave its name to the trial that made Bangladesh's founding father.
spotlights.memory_hook: The plot that was real, the trial that failed.

sections.title: Insurgency, a council and a peace deal
sections.intro_md:
Land was the core grievance. As settlers cleared and bought land in the valleys and foothills, tribal families who practised shifting cultivation lost ground, often without legal title. Two answers emerged. One was the ballot: the Communist movement, led by the tribal teacher Dasarath Deb, built a base among both tribal peasants and Bengali refugees, and the Left Front ruled Tripura for 35 of the 40 years from 1978. The other was the gun.

The Tripura National Volunteers fought from 1978 until a 1988 accord. Communal riots in June 1980 killed hundreds, most horrifically at Mandai. In the 1990s the National Liberation Front of Tripura and the All Tripura Tiger Force took up the fight, with camps in Bangladesh. The Armed Forces Special Powers Act was imposed in 1997 and lifted in 2015. A final accord in September 2024 brought the last armed groups in.

The lasting compromise is the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council, created in 1982 and placed under the Sixth Schedule in 1985.

NLFT and ATTF sign peace accord, 4 September

spotlights.name: Dasarath Deb
spotlights.spot_it: A young tribal activist in a 1946 photograph; later the only tribal Chief Minister Tripura has had.
spotlights.story_md: Born to a poor peasant family in Khowai, Dasarath Deb studied in Sylhet and Calcutta, then left his MA to run literacy campaigns among tribal villagers in the 1940s. In 1948 he founded the Ganamukti Parishad, which waged an armed struggle until 1950 and then joined the Communist Party. He was elected to the first Lok Sabha. From 1993 to 1998 he was Chief Minister, the first and so far only one from Tripura's indigenous peoples. His career explains a puzzle: why a state with deep tribal grievances voted Communist for decades.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He fused tribal rights with the Left and made it a mass movement.
spotlights.memory_hook: From night schools in the jungle to the CM's chair.

spotlights.name: The Mandai massacre
spotlights.spot_it: No memorial photograph survives on open record; the name is enough for most people in Tripura.
spotlights.story_md: In June 1980 tension over land and immigration exploded into riots across western Tripura. In the village of Mandai, about 30 km from Agartala, armed tribal militants surrounded the Bengali households on the night of 7 to 8 June and killed between 255 people, the official count, and 350 to 400, by other estimates. More than a thousand people, most of them Bengalis, died in the wider riots, and tribal villages suffered reprisals. The violence forced both communities into fortified, separate settlements and set the stage for twenty more years of conflict.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the darkest single event in Tripura's modern history.
spotlights.memory_hook: One night that divided a state.

spotlights.name: The 2024 peace accord

where.label: Signed in New Delhi; arms laid down at Jampuijala

spotlights.spot_it: Rows of surrendered rifles and fighters in uniform at a police battalion ground, three weeks after a signing in Delhi.
spotlights.story_md: On 4 September 2024 the Centre, the Tripura government and the NLFT and ATTF signed a memorandum of settlement in New Delhi, ending an armed movement that had run for about 34 years. The Centre promised a 250 crore rupee rehabilitation package. On 24 September cadres laid down their weapons at Jampuijala in Sepahijala district; reports put the number between about 330 and 584. The Chief Minister declared the state free of insurgency. The peace has politics attached: in June 2026 former militants blockaded roads and railways demanding faster delivery of the promised package.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It closed the last chapter of armed revolt in Tripura.
spotlights.memory_hook: Guns down in 2024, bills still being argued in 2026.

spotlights.name: Pradyot Bikram Manikya and TIPRA Motha
spotlights.spot_it: The former king's son, called Bubagra (king) by supporters, addressing huge rallies under the TIPRA Motha flag.
spotlights.story_md: Pradyot, born in 1978, is the son of Kirit Bikram, the last king. He led the state Congress briefly in 2019, quit, and turned a social organisation into TIPRA Motha, the Tipraha Indigenous Progressive Regional Alliance, in 2021. Its demand is 'Greater Tipraland', a separate state for indigenous people under Articles 2 and 3 of the Constitution. It won the tribal council in 2021, became the main opposition in the 2023 assembly with 13 seats, joined the BJP-led state government in March 2024, and then, contesting alone, won 24 of the 28 elected council seats in April 2026 with 57.6 percent of the vote.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The royal family is back at the centre of tribal politics, this time through elections.
spotlights.memory_hook: The king's grandson asks for votes, not tribute.

sections.title: Pitchers on heads, bamboo clappers and striped cloth
sections.intro_md:
Tripuri dance follows the farming year. Garia in April opens the sowing season, Lebang Boomani fills the wait for the monsoon, Mamita closes the harvest, and Hojagiri comes on the full moon after Durga Puja. The steps are mostly in the feet and hips, with the upper body held still, and the music is bamboo: the sumui flute, bamboo clappers, the kham drum and the sarinda and chongpreng, bowed and plucked strings.

The Chakma, Mog, Garo, Halam and Darlong peoples bring their own repertoires, and Bengali Agartala adds Rabindra Sangeet, Durga Puja theatre and a strong amateur drama culture.

Cloth carries identity. The striped rignai wrap, woven by women on loin looms, tells you which clan the wearer belongs to. Bamboo and cane, the state's commonest materials, become baskets, furniture, fans and carved figures.

spotlights.name: Hojagiri
spotlights.when: On the full moon after Durga Puja
spotlights.spot_it: Women stand on earthen pitchers or balance a bottle and a lit lamp on their heads while only their hips and legs move.
spotlights.story_md: Hojagiri belongs to the Reang, or Bru, and is performed by teams of four to six young women, with men singing and playing flute and drum. The dancers balance a bottle topped with a lit lamp on the head, hold lamps or plates in their hands and sometimes stand on the rim of a brass plate or an earthen pitcher, turning slowly while the upper body stays almost frozen. It honours the goddess Mailuma during the harvest Lakshmi Puja. Satyaram Reang, who spent decades teaching it, received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1986 and the Padma Shri in 2021; he died in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tripura's most famous dance and a test of balance few audiences forget.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hips dance, head stays still, the lamp never falls.

spotlights.name: Garia dance and Garia Puja
spotlights.when: Seven days from the first of Boishakh, mid-April
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers circle a decorated bamboo pole, the shrine of Baba Garia, with drums and flutes, moving from village to village.
spotlights.story_md: Garia Puja opens the Tripuri farming year in April. For seven days Kokborok-speaking tribes and the Halam worship Baba Garia, a god of prosperity, represented by a bamboo pole decked with cloth and flowers; a chicken is offered, and the Jamatia people hold a state-level mass celebration. The dance mimics the work ahead: clearing, sowing, birds and insects, building in tempo as the troupe goes house to house. Bengali, Chakma and other neighbours join in, and the pole-centred dance is one of the most recognisable images of Tripura.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the start of the agricultural and ritual year.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bamboo pole for a god, a whole village for a chorus.

spotlights.name: Lebang Boomani
spotlights.spot_it: Men beat bamboo clappers in quick patterns while women sweep colourful scarves to catch imaginary insects.
spotlights.story_md: After Garia, while the hill fields wait for rain, swarms of bright insects called lebang come down to eat the newly sown seed. In the dance, men play tokka, split-bamboo clappers, whose rhythm is meant to drive the lebang out of hiding, and women wave scarves to catch them. Villagers believed the number of lebang caught predicted the harvest. The music, with flute, kham and sarinda, is some of the liveliest in Tripuri repertoire.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns pest control into one of Tripura's most joyful dances.
spotlights.memory_hook: Catch the bugs, save the crop, keep the beat.

spotlights.name: Rignai and risa
spotlights.when: GI tags for risa and pachra-rignai in 2024
spotlights.spot_it: A striped wrap skirt (rignai) with a narrow woven band across the chest (risa), in clan-specific patterns.
spotlights.story_md: Tripuri women's dress has three parts: the rignai wrapped from the waist, the risa bound around the chest and the rikutu shawl. They are woven at home on the loin loom, where the weaver's body keeps the warp taut. Each clan once had its own rignai pattern, so a woman's clan could be read from her skirt. A legend says King Subrai married any woman who invented a new design and so collected 250. The white rignai with a maroon border, chamathwi bar, is worn for weddings and Garia. Risa is now given to honour guests, and in 2024 risa and the pachra-rignai received GI tags.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Cloth is the most visible everyday marker of Tripuri identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Read the stripes and you know the clan.

spotlights.name: Bamboo and cane

where.label: Workshops across the state; Agartala crafts emporia

spotlights.when: Everyday material, now a design product
spotlights.spot_it: Fine split-bamboo weaving for baskets, mats, lamps and chairs; figures carved from knotted bamboo roots.
spotlights.story_md: Bamboo grows everywhere in Tripura and is used for nearly everything: house frames, floors, fish traps, water carriers, musical instruments, the clappers of Lebang Boomani and the pole of Garia. Cane, a climbing palm, gives the strong strips for furniture. Craftspeople also carve the gnarled rhizomes into faces and gods. The state has pushed bamboo as an industry, from incense sticks to flooring, and its cane chairs and mats sell across India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the state's most ordinary and most versatile material.
spotlights.memory_hook: A grass that becomes a house, a song and a chair.

sections.title: Fermented fish, smoked pork and the sweetest pineapple
sections.intro_md:
Tripura eats two cuisines that share rice and fish. Bengali Tripura cooks the way Comilla and Sylhet do: rice, dal, fish curries, mustard, and sweets from milk. Tripuri food, borok chamung, is lighter on oil and spice and heavier on smoke, fermentation and greens from the forest and jhum field.

The key ingredient is berma, small fish such as puthi, dried and fermented in a sealed bamboo or clay pot until pungent. A little berma flavours stews, chutneys and the famous mui borok, the everyday Tripuri dish. Pork is smoked over the hearth; bamboo shoots, banana stem and wild herbs go into everything. Meals end with chuak, rice beer.

The fruit to know is the Queen pineapple: small, golden, very sweet, grown on the tillas and sold as far as the Gulf.

spotlights.name: Mui borok and berma
spotlights.spot_it: A plate of rice with small bowls of greens, bamboo shoot and a pungent, dark berma relish.
spotlights.story_md: Mui borok is less one recipe than the core of the Tripuri meal: seasonal vegetables, bamboo shoot or greens, cooked with little or no oil and flavoured with berma. Berma is made by sun-drying small fish, packing them tightly into a container and leaving them to ferment for months. The smell is strong; the taste is deep and savoury, like anchovy paste. Berma bwtwi is a stew of vegetables and berma. A mosdeng, a raw chutney of chilli, onion and herbs, sits on the side.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the taste most Tripuri people associate with home.
spotlights.memory_hook: A spoon of fermented fish carries the whole meal.

spotlights.name: Wahan mosdeng
spotlights.spot_it: Shreds of smoked or boiled pork tossed raw with chilli, onion, coriander and lime.
spotlights.story_md: Wahan means pork and mosdeng means a raw, pounded relish. The dish was once made with wild boar from the jungle; now it is farmed pork, smoked or boiled, then pulled into strips and mixed with green chilli, onion and herbs. It is hot, sharp and smoky, eaten with rice or flatbread and usually with chuak. In Bengali-majority Agartala, wahan mosdeng has become the signature 'tribal food' dish at festivals and on restaurant menus.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Tripuri dish outsiders are most likely to try first.
spotlights.memory_hook: Smoke, chilli and pork: the Tripura salad.

spotlights.name: Chuak
spotlights.spot_it: A cloudy, mildly sour rice beer poured from a bamboo tube or gourd at weddings and pujas.
spotlights.story_md: Chuak is made by fermenting cooked rice with a starter cake of herbs and yeast, then letting it stand. It is offered first to village elders at any ceremony, poured for guests, and is part of rituals from birth to cremation. Strength and taste vary from house to house; distilled, it becomes a much stronger spirit. Chuak is part of a belt of rice beers that runs across the North East and into Southeast Asia, from Assam's apong and Nagaland's zutho to Thailand's sato.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Sharing chuak is how hospitality and respect are shown.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rice in the field, rice in the cup.

spotlights.name: Queen pineapple

where.label: Hill slopes of West and South Tripura

spotlights.spot_it: A small golden pineapple with a rough, spiny skin and very sweet, crisp yellow flesh.
spotlights.story_md: Tripura grows the Queen and Kew varieties of pineapple on its tillas. The Queen is smaller than the familiar Kew, with a deep yellow flesh, high sugar and a strong aroma, and it holds a Geographical Indication tag. It is the state fruit and has reached export markets including the Middle East. In May 2026 the Centre and the state launched Mission Queen Pineapple, a three-year, 236 crore rupee plan for clusters, processing units, branding and export, with a hub near Agartala airport. Officials called the fruit a goodwill ambassador, and it already is one: every summer Bangladesh sends mangoes to Tripura and Tripura sends back Queen pineapples, most recently 600 fruit to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in July 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tripura's best chance at a famous food brand.
spotlights.memory_hook: Small, golden, and sent abroad as diplomacy.

sections.title: Fourteen gods, a closed capital and Durga in every lane
sections.intro_md:
Tripura's calendar mixes royal, tribal, Hindu, Buddhist and Bengali feasts. April brings three new years at once: Garia Puja for the Tripuri, Bizu for the Chakma and Sangrai for the Mog, alongside the Bengali Poila Boishakh. July and August belong to the royal-tribal rites of Kharchi and Ker. October is Durga Puja, as big in Agartala as in Kolkata, followed by Hojagiri on the full moon and the Diwali fair at Tripura Sundari.

The royal rites are unusual because they were never purely Hindu. Kharchi Puja worships fourteen gods with tribal priests called Chantai, and it is tied to an Earth-mother belief. The kings sponsored them for centuries and the state government still funds them, a direct survival of the old court into the present.

data.name: Pous Sankranti mela at Tirthamukh; Kokborok Day
Garia Puja, Bizu, Sangrai, Ashokastami at Unakoti
Durga Puja; Hojagiri on the full moon; Owa
Diwali fair at Tripura Sundari; Jampui orange festival

spotlights.name: Kharchi Puja
spotlights.spot_it: Fourteen small metal heads of gods carried in procession to the river by priests, then a week-long fair.
spotlights.story_md: Kharchi comes from khya, earth. Tripuri belief holds that the Earth mother menstruates during a period called Ama Pechi, when no one ploughs or digs. Fifteen days later Kharchi Puja cleanses her. At the Chaturdasha temple in Old Agartala, the old royal capital, the fourteen gods of the dynasty, represented only by heads, are carried by Chantai priests to the Saidra river, bathed and returned with flowers and vermilion. Goats and pigeons are sacrificed. Tribal and Bengali visitors fill a huge fair for seven days. The festival is funded by the state, which took over the duty from the kings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest royal festival is a tribal Earth rite in Hindu form.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fourteen heads, one river, a week of fair.

spotlights.name: Ker Puja, the day the capital shuts
spotlights.when: Two weeks after Kharchi, July or August
spotlights.spot_it: For about two and a half days a ritual boundary is drawn and the old capital's gates are closed.
spotlights.story_md: Ker is the guardian deity of the boundary. Two weeks after Kharchi, the Ker Puja draws a ritual boundary around the area being protected. Inside it, for roughly two and a half days, nobody may enter or leave, wear shoes, light a fire, dance or sing; in royal times the rule bound the king too. Halam participation is required. The rite was meant to protect the people and the state from disease, disaster and invasion, a quarantine in religious form, and it is still observed under state sponsorship.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare living example of a whole community observing a ritual lockdown.
spotlights.memory_hook: No shoes, no fire, no song, no one in or out.

spotlights.name: Durga Puja in Agartala
spotlights.spot_it: Lit pandals in every neighbourhood, and at the royal Durgabari a goddess with two arms showing instead of ten.
spotlights.story_md: Bengali Tripura celebrates Durga Puja on the Kolkata scale, with hundreds of themed pandals in Agartala alone and crowds into the small hours. The oldest and most special is at the Durgabari, a temple begun by the kings beside Ujjayanta Palace. Here Durga shows only two hands; the other eight are hidden behind her back. The story is that a queen of Krishna Kishore Manikya fainted at the sight of the ten-armed goddess, so the priests changed the image. Under the 1949 merger terms the state government pays for the daily worship, making Tripura probably the only state that funds a puja. On Dashami the Durgabari image is immersed first, with full state honours.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The state still performs a royal duty at Durgabari.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two arms showing, eight held back.

sections.title: How people live: literacy, the Left and the jhum field
sections.intro_md:
Two facts surprise most visitors. First, Tripura reads. Literacy rose from about 20 percent in 1961 to 87 percent in the 2011 census, among the highest in India, and in June 2025 the state was declared fully literate under the national ULLAS programme, at 95.6 percent, the third state to reach the mark after Mizoram and Goa. Volunteer teachers used primers in Bengali, English and Kokborok.

Second, politics here is intense and personal. The Left Front ran Tripura from 1978 to 1988 and from 1993 to 2018, the longest Communist rule anywhere in India after West Bengal. Party membership, not caste, shaped who got jobs and contracts, and elections often turned violent. The BJP's 2018 win ended 25 years of Left rule in one stroke.

In the hills, many families still combine settled rice farming with jhum, the rotational slash-and-burn system, now shrinking as rubber and pineapple plantations take over the slopes.

spotlights.name: Jhum, the moving field

where.label: Hill slopes across the TTAADC area

spotlights.spot_it: Patches of cleared, burnt hillside sown with rice, maize, sesame, cotton and vegetables mixed together.
spotlights.story_md: In jhum a family clears a patch of forest in winter, burns it in the dry season and, after Garia Puja, dibbles a mix of seeds into the ash: hill rice, maize, millet, sesame, cotton, gourds and chillies. After a year or two the plot is left to regrow and the family moves on, returning when the forest has recovered. With long fallows it is sustainable; with more people and less land the cycle shortens and soils wear out. Tripura's dances, festivals and calendar are built around jhum, but the state has spent decades moving jhumias into rubber, tea and settled rice in the lungas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of tribal culture grew out of this farming cycle, which is now disappearing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Burn, sow, harvest, walk on, come back in ten years.

spotlights.name: Manik Sarkar, the poorest chief minister
spotlights.spot_it: A slight man in a white kurta, famous for living in a government flat and walking to meetings.
spotlights.story_md: Manik Sarkar, son of a tailor, joined the CPI(M) at 19 and became Chief Minister in 1998, winning four elections in a row. He handed his salary to the party and lived on an allowance it paid him back. In 2018 an analysis by the Association for Democratic Reforms of every chief minister's sworn assets ranked him the poorest in India, with total assets of about 27 lakh rupees and a bank balance of 2,410 rupees. His government won praise for ending the insurgency and lifting literacy, and criticism for slow growth and a party-controlled state. The Left lost power in 2018, and he did not contest in 2023.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He became a national symbol of personal honesty in politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty years in power, a few thousand rupees in the bank.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
For a state of under four million, Tripura has produced a remarkable spread of people: a dynasty of composers, a gymnast who nearly won India's first Olympic medal in her sport, Asian Games tennis gold, dancers honoured with the Padma Shri, and chief ministers with very different ideas of government.

Some of them, like S. D. Burman, made their names far from Agartala and are claimed by Bengal and Bombay as well. Others, like Dipa Karmakar, trained in Agartala's modest halls and became national stories. Politicians on this list include Dasarath Deb and Manik Sarkar, covered earlier, the BJP's Biplab Kumar Deb, Chief Minister from 2018 to 2022, and Manik Saha, a dental surgeon who succeeded him in May 2022 and is also president of the Tripura Cricket Association.

spotlights.name: Dipa Karmakar
spotlights.spot_it: A small, powerful vaulter landing the Produnova, the 'vault of death': a handspring and two front somersaults.
spotlights.story_md: Dipa began gymnastics at six in Agartala with flat feet, a serious handicap for a gymnast, and trained the arches into them. Coached by Bishweshwar Nandi, she won Commonwealth Games bronze in 2014, the first Indian woman to win a gymnastics medal there, and became one of only five women ever to land the Produnova, a vault rated 7.0 in difficulty. At Rio 2016 she was the first Indian woman gymnast at an Olympics and finished fourth in the vault final with 15.066, 0.15 behind bronze. In 2018 she won gold at a World Challenge Cup in Turkey. She retired in 2024.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She put Indian gymnastics, and Agartala, on the world stage.
spotlights.memory_hook: Flat feet, the vault of death and 0.15 of a point.

spotlights.name: Somdev Devvarman
spotlights.spot_it: A fast, fit baseline player with a big forehand and a Tripura royal-family surname.
spotlights.story_md: Somdev Devvarman, whose family has its roots in Tripura, played college tennis at the University of Virginia, where he won two NCAA singles titles, and turned professional in 2008. In 2010 he won singles gold at the Commonwealth Games in Delhi and then singles and doubles gold at the Asian Games in Guangzhou, the first Indian man to win the Asian Games singles title. He reached the final of the Chennai Open as a wild card in 2009 and was a mainstay of India's Davis Cup team. He received the Arjuna Award in 2011 and the Padma Shri in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that an Indian singles player could win at Asian level.
spotlights.memory_hook: First Indian to win Asian Games singles gold.

sections.title: Rubber, gas and a door to the sea
sections.intro_md:
Tripura's economy is small and mostly rural. The state's output in 2022 to 2023 was about 640 billion rupees at constant prices, growing about 10 percent that year; per capita income was around 158,000 rupees, below the national 197,000. More than half the people live off farming, yet only about 27 percent of the land can be cultivated, and rice takes 91 percent of the cropped area.

The cash comes from rubber, where Tripura is second only to Kerala, from tea, bamboo, fish farming and agarwood, and from the natural gas under its hills, which feeds power plants that made Tripura a power-surplus state from 2014.

The great constraint has always been distance. The answer now being built is to go through Bangladesh: a bridge to Chittagong port, a rail link to Akhaura, an international airport, and the hope of turning a dead end into a corridor.

data.metric: Via Maitri Setu and Chittagong (planned freight route)

spotlights.name: Rubber on the tillas
spotlights.spot_it: Neat rows of grey-barked trees with a spiral cut and a cup collecting white latex, and sheets drying on lines.
spotlights.story_md: Rubber came to Tripura in the 1960s as a way to settle jhum families and stop soil erosion on the hills, and it took off. Tripura is now India's second-largest producer of natural rubber after Kerala, though far behind it: Rubber Board figures in 2018 put the state at about 10 percent of India's rubber area and 9 percent of output. Tribal and Bengali smallholders tap trees at dawn, roll the coagulated latex into sheets and smoke them. In recent years the state has exported rubber to Bangladesh and Nepal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It changed hill farming more than anything since jhum.
spotlights.memory_hook: White milk at dawn, brown sheets by noon.

spotlights.name: Agarwood, the scented resin
spotlights.spot_it: Dark, resin-streaked heartwood sold by the gram, and oil worth more than its weight in silver.
spotlights.story_md: When an Aquilaria tree is wounded and infected by a fungus, it fills its heartwood with a dark, fragrant resin. That resinous wood, agar or oud, is burned as incense and distilled into oil for perfumes sold in the Gulf and East Asia, where the best grades fetch extraordinary prices. Agartala's very name comes from the tree. Tripura farmers now plant it widely and inoculate trees to induce the resin. A 2021 state policy aimed to double plantations by 2025 and estimated a potential trade of about 2,000 crore rupees a year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The tree that named the capital could become one of its richest crops.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wounded tree that bleeds perfume.

spotlights.name: Palatana gas power plant
spotlights.spot_it: Two gas turbines and a stack in the Gomati hills, the biggest power plant in the North East.
spotlights.story_md: Tripura sits on large reserves of natural gas, estimated by ONGC at about 400 billion cubic metres in place, though only a small part is recoverable. Until 2014 the state still had power shortages. Then the 726.6 MW ONGC Tripura Power Company plant at Palatana came fully on line, its second unit dedicated in November 2014. It is the largest single power plant in the North East and turned Tripura into a surplus state, able to supply neighbours and Bangladesh. Getting the turbines in was itself diplomacy: Bangladesh let the 80-tonne loads travel by river from Haldia to its port at Ashuganj and then 49 km by road to Akhaura, building 16 diversions round weak bridges, because the Indian hill route could not carry them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gas turned an energy-poor state into an exporter of power.
spotlights.memory_hook: The biggest power plant in the North East, delivered through Bangladesh.

spotlights.name: Maitri Setu
spotlights.spot_it: A single-span concrete bridge over the Feni river linking Sabroom to Ramgarh in Bangladesh.
spotlights.story_md: The Friendship Bridge is 150 m long, 1.9 km with approaches, and was built by India at a cost of about 133 crore rupees. It joins NH-8 at Sabroom, Tripura's southern tip and its last railway station, to Ramgarh in Bangladesh, from where Chittagong port is only about 80 km away. The aim is to give landlocked North East India a short route to the sea: Agartala to Kolkata port via Chittagong is roughly 450 km, against more than 1,600 km round the Siliguri corridor, and logistics costs could fall sharply. Modi and Sheikh Hasina opened it by video link on 9 March 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tripura's bid to stop being a dead end.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 150 m bridge that could save 1,000 km.

spotlights.name: The Agartala-Akhaura rail link
spotlights.spot_it: A new viaduct running west from Agartala station straight to the border, with a monument on the Bangladesh side.
spotlights.story_md: The 12.24 km line, 5.46 km in India and 6.78 km in Bangladesh, all paid for by India, connects Agartala to Akhaura junction on Bangladesh's main Dhaka-Chittagong line. It was meant to cut the rail trip from Kolkata from about 31 hours to about 10. The Indian side includes a 3.7 km viaduct to spare farmland. Modi and Hasina inaugurated it virtually on 1 November 2023 after a trial run in September, but passenger and freight services never began. After the change of government in Dhaka in August 2024, India halted further work in April 2025; in October 2026 Northeast Frontier Railway said it would speed up pending works.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A finished line with no trains shows how politics can stop geography.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twelve kilometres, inaugurated, waiting.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Fly to Agartala from Kolkata, Delhi, Guwahati or Bengaluru, or take the train through Assam. Most sights fit into a five-day loop. Start in Agartala with Ujjayanta Palace and its museum, the Durgabari and the Chaturdasha temple in Old Agartala. Drive south to Neermahal on Rudrasagar, then to Udaipur for Tripura Sundari and the Bhubaneswari temple. Take a boat to the Chabimura carvings near Amarpur and, if you have a day, go on to Pilak and the far south at Sabroom. The north needs its own trip: Unakoti near Kailashahar and the Jampui Hills, best in October and November when the oranges ripen.

The best months are October to March. Summer is hot and humid and the monsoon brings floods and landslides on the hill roads.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Tripura's news since 2024 has been shaped by Bangladesh, by tribal politics and by a few milestones.

The fall of Sheikh Hasina's government in Dhaka in August 2024 chilled relations with India, and Tripura felt it first. Floods that month killed more than 20 people in the state and set off accusations from Bangladesh about the Dumboor dam, which India rejected. In December 2024 protesters broke into the Bangladesh Assistant High Commission in Agartala; India called it deeply regrettable. Rail and trade projects stalled.

At home, the last insurgent groups signed a peace accord in September 2024. The state was declared fully literate in June 2025. The Prime Minister opened the rebuilt Tripura Sundari temple complex in September 2025. In April 2026 TIPRA Motha, contesting without its BJP ally, swept the tribal council. In May 2026 a 236 crore rupee mission for the Queen pineapple began, and in July the yearly pineapple gift went to Bangladesh's new prime minister.

spotlights.name: The 2026 tribal council election
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds in white and maroon TIPRA colours; a council covering two-thirds of the state's land.
spotlights.story_md: The Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council governs about 7,133 square km, two-thirds of the state, from its headquarters at Khumulwng. In April 2026 about 963,000 voters chose 28 members. TIPRA Motha, still a partner in the state government, refused to share seats with the BJP and won 24 seats with 57.6 percent of the vote; the BJP took the other 4, and the Left, which ran the council for years, won none and failed to reach 10 percent. The result gives Pradyot's party a firmer claim to speak for indigenous Tripura as the 2028 assembly election approaches.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows tribal voters consolidating behind a regional party.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-four of twenty-eight, and a royal at the head.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
A few things people often get wrong about Tripura, and what the evidence says.

Tripura is not part of Bangladesh, and never was: it was a princely state that kept its own kings under the British and joined India in 1947 to 1949. It is not 'all tribal': two-thirds of people are Bengali-speaking. The royal line did not rule for 2,000 years in any provable sense: the Rajmala's early kings are legend, and the documented dynasty begins around 1400. Unakoti does not hold 99,99,999 carvings: that is the legend's number, and the real count is a few hundred. And the Left did not rule Tripura without a break from 1978: Congress and the Tripura Upajati Juba Samiti governed from 1988 to 1993.

The table sets out the main claims.

sections.title: Recap: Tripura in eight lines
sections.intro_md:
1. Third-smallest state, with Bangladesh on three sides along 856 km.
2. The Manikya kings ruled from about 1400 to 1949; the Rajmala's early kings are legend.
3. A Tripuri court with Bengali culture, patron of Tagore, who came seven times.
4. Refugees after 1947 and 1971 made tribal people a minority; the insurgency that followed ended with a 2024 accord.
5. Gods in the hills: Unakoti, Chabimura, Pilak, and Tripura Sundari's temple of 1501.
6. Hojagiri balances pitchers and lamps; rignai stripes name the clan; berma flavours the food.
7. Rubber, gas, agarwood and the Queen pineapple; Bangladesh is the short road to the sea.
8. Fully literate since 2025, with the former royal family leading the tribal council by vote.

best_facts.fact: Before 1947 the road from Agartala to Kolkata was under 350 km; after Partition the Indian route grew to about 1,700 km, all the way round Bangladesh.
best_facts.why_surprising: A line on a map multiplied a journey by five.

best_facts.fact: In 1971 the number of refugees in Tripura roughly matched the state's own population of about 1.5 million.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state effectively doubled in a few months.

best_facts.fact: Pakistan's 1968 treason case against Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was named the Agartala Conspiracy Case, after the Indian town where the plot was said to be hatched; in 2011 one accused said it was true.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bangladesh's founding trial carries an Indian town's name.

best_facts.fact: Maharaja Bir Chandra Manikya was a serious photographer and held an annual photo exhibition in his palace, the first such royal show in India; his studio was rediscovered a century later.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 19th-century hill king behind the camera.

side_dish.title: Sacred groves and holy ponds: when belief protects wildlife
side_dish.body_md:
The black softshell turtles of Kalyan Sagar are not a one-off. Across South Asia, religious taboo has protected nature where law could not. Ecologists call these places **sacred natural sites**: groves, ponds and hills set aside for a deity, where cutting, hunting or fishing is forbidden.

India has tens of thousands of sacred groves, from the *kavu* of Kerala and the *devrai* of Maharashtra to the *law kyntang* of Meghalaya. Studies often find them richer in old trees, medicinal plants and rare species than the surrounding land, because they have been left alone for centuries. Sacred ponds play the same role for animals like the Bostami turtle, which was declared extinct in the wild in 2002 and survives mainly in shrine ponds in Bangladesh and North East India.

The protection is real but fragile. Feeding turtles bread and sweets harms them; temple renovations can concrete over nesting banks; and when belief weakens, the taboo goes. Conservationists now work *with* temple committees: collecting eggs from shrine ponds, hatching them and releasing young turtles into the wild.

The lesson is a practical one. Protected areas run by the state cover only about 5 percent of India. A far larger network of small places is protected because people think they belong to the gods. Counting and caring for them is one of the cheapest conservation tools there is.

offline_task.title: Make a quick wahan mosdeng (or its vegetarian cousin)
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 2. About 30 minutes.** Mosdeng is the Tripuri raw relish: smoky, hot and sharp.

**You need**
- 250 g pork belly or shoulder (or for a vegetarian version: 2 brinjals, roasted whole over a flame)
- 1 small red onion, very finely sliced
- 3 to 4 green chillies, finely chopped (fewer if you are cautious)
- A handful of fresh coriander, chopped
- Half a lime
- Salt
- Optional, for the real taste: half a teaspoon of fish sauce to stand in for berma

**Method**
1. Boil the pork in salted water for about 20 minutes until cooked through. Drain and dry it.
2. For smoke, char the pieces in a dry pan or straight over a gas flame until the edges blacken. (For the vegetarian version, char the brinjals until soft, peel and mash.)
3. Slice the pork into thin strips or shred it with two forks.
4. Crush the chillies with a pinch of salt in a mortar, or press with the back of a spoon.
5. Toss the pork with onion, chillies, coriander, lime and the optional fish sauce. Taste: it should be hot, salty and sharp.
6. Eat with plain rice.

As you eat, note the absence of oil and spice blends. That is the point of Tripuri hill cooking: smoke, chilli and fermentation do the work.
